title: Unit 4f - Maze Project Introduction
summary: Title slide introducing the Maze Project unit in CS 103, covering breadth-first search and maze solving. Presented by Mark Redekopp.
main_text: This is the title slide for Unit 4f on the Maze Project in the CS 103 course. This unit covers breadth-first search (BFS), its application to graph traversal and shortest path finding, and a maze-solving project that applies BFS along with file I/O, dynamic memory allocation, and object-oriented design principles.
notes_text: The Maze Project is a significant programming assignment that integrates many concepts from previous units: linked lists for the queue, file I/O for reading maze files, 2D dynamic arrays, and classes for encapsulation.

title: Path Planning - Finding the Shortest Path
summary: Revisits path planning from Unit 0: when the finish location is unknown, squares should be examined in order of proximity to find the shortest path.
main_text: What if you do not know where the Finish square is? You can examine any square (no longer a robot) one at a time, in any order. The question is: in what order would you examine the locations to find the shortest path to the goal location? The diagram shows an 8x8 grid with S (start) at position (3,2) and question marks at several locations (1,2), (2,5), and (6,3) representing possible finish locations. The key insight is that to guarantee finding the shortest path, you must examine squares in order of their distance from the start.
notes_text: This revisits a concept from Unit 0 and provides motivation for BFS. The grid-based maze is a concrete example of a more general graph search problem.

images.description: 8x8 grid with S at position (3,2) and question marks at three locations, representing unknown finish positions. The grid has walls shown as dark cells.

title: Path Planning - Breadth-First Approach
summary: Shows that examining closer squares before further ones guarantees finding the shortest path, which is the breadth-first search strategy.
main_text: To find the shortest path when you do not know where the finish is, examine all closer squares one at a time before progressing to further squares. The diagram shows the grid with numbers indicating distance from S: squares at distance 1 are colored green/yellow, distance 2 are orange, distance 3 are colored differently. If you do not know where F (finish) is and want to find the shortest path, you should examine all closer locations before examining further-away locations. This is called uninformed search for shortest path, specifically Breadth-first search. The finish F is found at distance 3 from S. The key principle is: explore all locations at distance d before any locations at distance d+1.
notes_text: Breadth-first search guarantees the shortest path in an unweighted graph because it explores all nodes at depth k before any nodes at depth k+1. This property makes it ideal for maze solving where all moves have equal cost.

images.description: Grid showing BFS exploration with numbered cells indicating distance from start S. Cells colored by distance: green for 1, yellow/orange for 2, further for 3. F found at distance 3.

title: BFS (Shortest Distance) With Graphs Section Divider
summary: Section divider transitioning to breadth-first search applied to graphs for finding shortest distances.
main_text: This is a section divider slide marking the transition to BFS (Shortest Distance) With Graphs. The following slides generalize BFS from grid-based mazes to arbitrary graph structures with vertices and edges.
notes_text: Generalizing from grids to graphs is important because BFS applies to any structure where nodes have neighbors, not just 2D grids.

title: Breadth-First Search on Graphs
summary: Generalizes BFS to arbitrary graphs with vertices and edges, starting from vertex u and fanning out to find minimum hops to every other vertex.
main_text: Now we generalize BFS to an arbitrary set of connections/neighbors. Given a graph with vertices V and edges E, and a starting vertex u, BFS starts at u ('a' in the diagram) and fans out along the edges to nearest neighbors, then to their neighbors, and so on. The goal is to find the minimum number of hops (also known as depth or distance) from the start vertex to every other vertex. The diagram shows a graph with 8 vertices (a through h) connected by edges. Vertex 'a' is highlighted as the starting vertex u, at depth 0.
notes_text: Graphs are a fundamental data structure in computer science. BFS on graphs has many applications beyond maze solving, including social network analysis, web crawling, and network routing.

images.description: Graph with 8 vertices labeled a through h connected by edges. Vertex 'a' is highlighted in orange as the starting vertex u at depth 0. Edges connect: a-b, a-c, a-e, b-c, b-h, c-d, c-g, d-e, d-f, e-f, f-g.

title: BFS Graph Traversal - Complete Example
summary: Shows complete BFS traversal of a graph, discovering vertices layer by layer: depth 0 is a, depth 1 is c and e, depth 2 is b, d, f, g, and depth 3 is h.
main_text: Three stages of BFS traversal are shown on the same graph. First, starting from vertex a (depth 0), we discover its neighbors c and e at depth 1. Next, exploring c and e, we discover their unvisited neighbors b, d, f, and g at depth 2. Finally, exploring those depth-2 vertices, we discover h at depth 3. The complete depth assignments are: Depth 0: a. Depth 1: c, e. Depth 2: b, d, f, g. Depth 3: h. Each vertex is colored to indicate when it was discovered, with depth numbers shown next to each vertex. This demonstrates how BFS systematically explores the graph level by level.
notes_text: Notice that BFS processes ALL vertices at the current depth before moving to the next depth. This is what guarantees shortest paths. The order within a depth level depends on the order neighbors are processed, but the depth assignment is always optimal.

images.description: Three copies of the same graph showing progressive BFS discovery. Left: depth 0 (a) and depth 1 (c, e) discovered. Center: depth 2 (b, d, f, g) discovered. Right: depth 3 (h) discovered. All vertices colored orange when discovered with depth numbers.

title: Developing the BFS Algorithm - Key Idea
summary: Establishes the key BFS requirement: must explore all nearer neighbors before further-away neighbors, which means using a FIFO queue.
main_text: The key idea of BFS is that we must explore all nearer neighbors before exploring further-away neighbors. From vertex 'a' we find neighbors 'e' and 'c'. Since a computer can only do one thing at a time, we have to pick either e or c to explore first. If we pick e, we find f. Now what vertex should we explore (visit neighbors) next? The choices are c and f. The answer is c, because c is at depth 1 while f is at depth 2. If we do not explore c first, we will not find shortest paths (for example, to vertex d). We must explore all vertices at depth i before any vertices at depth i+1. This ordering requirement leads directly to the need for a FIFO (First-In, First-Out) data structure.
notes_text: This slide builds intuition for WHY a queue is needed. If we used a stack (LIFO) instead, we would get depth-first search, which does not guarantee shortest paths. The FIFO property of a queue ensures that earlier-discovered (closer) vertices are processed before later-discovered (farther) ones.

images.description: Graph showing partial BFS from vertex a. Vertex a (depth 0) has discovered e (depth 1) and c (depth 1). From e, f (depth 2) is discovered. The question asks which to explore next: c or f, with c being correct.

title: Developing the BFS Algorithm - Queue and Marking
summary: Introduces the BFS data structure requirements: a FIFO queue for ordering exploration, and marking vertices to avoid revisiting them.
main_text: To implement BFS, we need to keep a first-in / first-out list (also known as FIFO, queue, or deque) of neighbors found. We pull vertices out of the front of the list and explore their neighbors. When we find a new neighboring vertex, we add it to the back of the list. Critically, we do not want to put a vertex in the queue more than once, so we need to mark a vertex the first time we encounter it. We will only allow unmarked vertices to be put in the queue. This marking prevents infinite loops and ensures each vertex is processed exactly once.
notes_text: The queue is the fundamental data structure that makes BFS work. The deque from Unit 4d is ideal here since we need push_back and pop_front, both O(1). The marking/visited mechanism is essential for correctness and termination.

title: BFS Initialization
summary: Shows BFS initialization: set all vertex depths to -1 (unvisited), create queue Q, add start vertex u, and mark u as visited with depth 0.
main_text: The BFS algorithm initialization (BFS(Gr, u)): First, initialize all vertices as 'not visited' by setting depth = -1. A depth of -1 means we have NOT visited the vertex, while a depth >= 0 means we have visited it AND know its distance from the start. Next, create a queue (list) Q. Add the start vertex u to Q. Mark u as 'visited' by setting its depth to 0. The diagram shows the graph with vertex 'a' highlighted in yellow (depth = 0) and all other vertices showing depth = -1. The queue Q contains just 'a'. This setup prepares for the main BFS loop.
notes_text: Using -1 as the 'unvisited' sentinel is a common pattern. It serves double duty: tracking whether a vertex has been discovered AND storing the actual distance once discovered. This eliminates the need for a separate visited boolean array.

images.description: Graph with vertex 'a' marked at depth 0 (yellow/green), all other vertices at depth -1 (gray). Queue Q shown below containing only 'a'.

title: BFS Algorithm - Main Loop and First Iteration
summary: Presents the complete BFS algorithm with its main while loop, and shows the first iteration where vertex a is dequeued and its neighbors c and e are discovered.
main_text: The complete BFS algorithm: Initialize all vertices as unvisited by setting their depth = -1. Create a list Q. Add start vertex u to Q. Mark u as visited with depth = 0. Then enter the main loop: while Q is not empty, remove the front item and call it x. For each neighbor y of x, if vertex y is not found (depth == -1), add y to back of the list Q, and mark y as found by setting depth of y = depth of x + 1. In the first iteration, x = a (dequeued from front). Vertex a's neighbors are c and e. Both have depth -1 (unvisited), so both are added to Q with depth = 0 + 1 = 1. After this iteration: Q contains [e, c], c has depth 1, e has depth 1.
notes_text: The depth calculation 'depth of y = depth of x + 1' is what ensures correct shortest-path distances. Each newly discovered vertex is exactly one hop further from the start than the vertex that discovered it.

images.description: Graph showing first BFS iteration: x = a (orange, dequeued), c and e discovered at depth 1 (blue labels 'y'). Queue Q shown with [e, c]. Depths updated: a=0, c=1, e=1, others=-1.

title: BFS Algorithm - Processing Depth 1 Vertices
summary: Shows BFS processing vertices e and c at depth 1, discovering f from e and b, d, g from c, all assigned depth 2.
main_text: Continuing the BFS: when x = e (dequeued from front), we examine e's neighbors. Vertex a is already visited (depth 0), so we skip it. Vertex f has depth -1, so we add f to Q and set f's depth to 1 + 1 = 2. Queue becomes [c, f]. Next, x = c (dequeued from front). Vertex c's neighbors include a (depth 0, skip), e (depth 1, skip), and unvisited vertices b, d, and g. All three are added to Q with depth = 1 + 1 = 2. Queue becomes [f, b, d, g]. After processing all depth-1 vertices: depths are a=0, c=1, e=1, b=2, d=2, f=2, g=2, h=-1.
notes_text: Notice how the queue naturally ensures all depth-1 vertices (e, c) are processed before any depth-2 vertices (f, b, d, g). This is the key property that makes BFS correct for shortest paths.

images.description: Two graph states showing: processing e discovers f at depth 2, then processing c discovers b, d, g at depth 2. Queue contents shown at each step.

title: BFS Algorithm - Processing Depth 2 Vertices and Completion
summary: Shows BFS processing depth-2 vertices f, b, d, g, discovering h at depth 3 from b, completing the traversal.
main_text: Processing depth-2 vertices: x = f is dequeued. Its neighbors (d, e, g) are all already visited, so nothing new is added. x = b is dequeued. Its neighbors include a (visited) and c (visited), but h has depth -1. So h is added to Q with depth = 2 + 1 = 3. Queue becomes [d, g, h]. x = d is dequeued. All neighbors (c, e, f, g) are already visited. Nothing added. x = g is dequeued. All neighbors already visited. x = h is dequeued. All neighbors already visited. Queue is now empty, loop terminates. Final depths: a=0, c=1, e=1, b=2, d=2, f=2, g=2, h=3. These represent the minimum number of hops from vertex a to each other vertex.
notes_text: The BFS is complete when the queue becomes empty. At this point, every reachable vertex has been assigned its correct shortest distance from the start. Unreachable vertices would still have depth = -1.

images.description: Final graph state with all vertices colored and labeled with depths: a=0, c=1, e=1, b=2, d=2, f=2, g=2, h=3. Queue is empty.

title: Queue Implementation for BFS
summary: Identifies that BFS needs push_back and pop_front operations, making a deque the appropriate data structure for the queue.
main_text: The BFS algorithm requires specific operations on the queue: while Q is not empty, remove the front item (pop_front), and for each unvisited neighbor, add it to the back of the list (push_back). The question is: what operations do we need to perform on our queue? We need push_back (add to end) and pop_front (remove from front). What data structure would be appropriate? A deque, since it supports O(1) push_back and pop_front. This connects directly to the deque data structure studied in Unit 4d.
notes_text: This is a practical application of the deque from Unit 4d. The queue could also be implemented with a linked list (singly-linked with tail pointer supports O(1) push_back and pop_front). The C++ deque<T> class or a custom linked-list queue both work.

images.description: Graph showing BFS state with queue containing [f, b, d, g], demonstrating the push_back/pop_front pattern needed for BFS.

title: Maze Project Section Divider
summary: Section divider transitioning from general BFS on graphs to the specific maze-solving project application.
main_text: This is a section divider slide marking the transition to the Maze Project. The following slides apply BFS to solving mazes represented as 2D grids, where S marks the start, F marks the finish, dots are open paths, and pound signs are walls.
notes_text: The maze is essentially a grid graph where each cell is a vertex and edges connect adjacent non-wall cells.

title: Maze Solver - Problem Setup
summary: Defines the maze format: S=Start, F=Finish, dot=Free, pound=Wall, and the goal is to find the shortest path from S to F using BFS.
main_text: Consider this maze where S = Start, F = Finish, . (dot) = Free path, and # (pound sign) = Wall. The goal is to find the shortest path from S to F. The example 4x4 maze shows: row 0 is all dots (open), row 1 has S at (1,0), wall at (1,1), F at (1,2), wall at (1,3), row 2 has dot, wall, dot, wall, row 3 has dot, dot, dot, wall. Each cell is identified by its (row, column) coordinates. The neighbors of each cell are the four adjacent cells: North (row-1), West (col-1), South (row+1), East (col+1).
notes_text: The maze is stored as a 2D character array. Valid moves are to adjacent non-wall cells that are within bounds. This is equivalent to a graph where vertices are non-wall cells and edges connect adjacent open cells.

images.description: 4x4 maze grid with coordinates (row,col) labeled. S at (1,0), F at (1,2), walls (#) at (1,1), (1,3), (2,1), (2,3), (3,3). Open cells shown as dots.

title: BFS Applied to Maze - Algorithm Overview
summary: Applies BFS to the maze: create a queue, add start location, loop extracting front and adding valid unvisited neighbors until finish is found.
main_text: Fact 1: Computers can only do 1 thing at a time, so since we cannot explore all squares at once, we must save some locations until we can process them. To do this we use the breadth-first search algorithm. The BFS Algorithm for mazes: Create a list or queue (linked list). Add the start location to the queue. Loop until the queue is empty (or you find your goal): extract the front element, generate/loop through its neighbors (N,W,S,E), and add each neighbor to the BACK of the list/queue if it has not been seen before. The diagram shows the maze with BFS exploration labels: cells labeled 1A (distance 1 from S), 1B, 1C, 1D (distance 1 in different directions), 2A, 2B, 2C (distance 2), indicating the order of exploration.
notes_text: The maze BFS is identical to graph BFS, with the grid providing the neighbor structure. Each cell's neighbors are its four cardinal direction adjacents (N, W, S, E) that are within bounds and not walls.

images.description: Maze grid showing BFS exploration order with cells labeled 1A through 2C indicating distance and discovery order from start S. Queue shown below with S as initial element.

title: Maze Solver - BFS with Visited and Predecessor Arrays
summary: Shows the maze solver uses three data structures: maze array, visited array, and predecessor array to track exploration and enable path reconstruction.
main_text: The maze solver begins by putting the starting location into the queue. It maintains three data structures: the Maze array (the actual maze characters), a Visited array (tracking which cells have been explored, initialized to all 0s with the start set to 1), and a Predecessor array (recording which cell discovered each cell, initialized to -1,-1). The algorithm loop: extract the front location as 'curr', visit each neighbor (N,W,S,E) one at a time. If the neighbor is the finish, stop and trace backwards. Else if the neighbor is a valid location (in bounds, not a wall) and not visited before, then add it to the back of the queue, mark it as visited (set to 1), and record its predecessor (set to curr). The queue uses a linked list with HEAD pointer.
notes_text: The predecessor array is crucial for reconstructing the actual path, not just finding the distance. Each cell records which cell led to its discovery, creating a chain from finish back to start. The visited array prevents infinite loops.

images.description: Complete maze solver state showing: 4x4 maze array, queue as linked list with HEAD pointer containing (1,0), 4x4 Visited array (initialized to 0s, start at 1), and 4x4 Predecessor array (initialized to -1,-1).

title: Maze Solver - BFS Step-by-Step Trace (Part 1)
summary: Traces BFS through the maze: dequeuing S at (1,0), discovering neighbors (0,0) and (2,0), then processing those to discover (0,1) and (3,0).
main_text: Step-by-step trace of BFS on the 4x4 maze. Starting state: Queue has (1,0), Visited[1][0]=1. Iteration 1: curr = (1,0), dequeued from front. Check neighbors N=(0,0): valid and unvisited, add to queue, mark visited, set predecessor to (1,0). W=out of bounds. S=(2,0): valid and unvisited, add to queue, mark visited, set predecessor to (1,0). E=(1,1): wall, skip. Queue now: [(0,0), (2,0)]. Iteration 2: curr = (0,0). Neighbors: N=out of bounds. W=out of bounds. S=(1,0): already visited, skip. E=(0,1): valid and unvisited, add to queue, set predecessor to (0,0). Queue: [(2,0), (0,1)]. Visited and Predecessor arrays updated accordingly.
notes_text: Each iteration dequeues from the front and checks four neighbors in order (N, W, S, E). The predecessor of each newly discovered cell is always the cell that was being processed (curr) when it was found.

images.description: Maze solver state after processing (1,0) and (0,0). Queue contains remaining items. Visited array shows 1s for discovered cells. Predecessor array shows which cell discovered each.

title: Maze Solver - BFS Step-by-Step Trace (Part 2)
summary: Continues BFS trace: processing (2,0) discovers (3,0), processing (0,1) discovers (0,2), and exploration continues until finding finish F.
main_text: Continuing the BFS trace: curr = (2,0). Neighbors: N=(1,0) visited, W=out of bounds, S=(3,0) valid and unvisited (add to queue, predecessor=(2,0)), E=(2,1) is wall. curr = (0,1). Neighbors: N=out of bounds, W=(0,0) visited, S=(1,1) wall, E=(0,2) valid and unvisited (add to queue, predecessor=(0,1)). curr = (3,0). Neighbors: S=out of bounds, E=(3,1) valid and unvisited (add to queue, predecessor=(3,0)). curr = (0,2). Neighbors: checking E neighbor at (0,2)'s east is (0,3). But critically, checking S neighbor: (1,2) = F, the Finish! Found the Finish at (1,2). The predecessor of (1,2) is set to (0,2), which was the current cell when F was discovered.
notes_text: The BFS finds the finish when it encounters F as a neighbor of the current cell being processed. At this point, the predecessor chain from F back to S gives the shortest path.

images.description: Maze solver state when finish F at (1,2) is found as a neighbor of curr=(0,2). Queue and Predecessor arrays show the complete state at discovery time.

title: Maze Solver - Path Backtracking
summary: After finding the finish, uses the predecessor array to trace backwards from F to S, marking the shortest path with asterisks.
main_text: Now we need to backtrack and add '*' characters to mark the shortest path. We use the predecessor array to walk backwards from the finish (curr) to the start. The algorithm: set maze[curr] = '*' (mark current cell as part of path), then update curr to its predecessor (curr = predecessor[curr]). Repeat until we reach the start. Tracing from the finish at (1,2): predecessor of (1,2) is (0,2), so mark (0,2) with '*' and move to (0,2). Predecessor of (0,2) is (0,1), so mark (0,1) with '*' and move to (0,1). Predecessor of (0,1) is (0,0), so mark (0,0) with '*' and move to (0,0). Predecessor of (0,0) is (1,0) which is the start S. The shortest path is: S(1,0) -> (0,0) -> (0,1) -> (0,2) -> F(1,2), marked with asterisks in the maze array.
notes_text: The backtracking phase is simple and O(path_length). It follows the predecessor chain like a linked list from finish to start. The '*' markers create a visual representation of the shortest path in the maze output.

images.description: Three stages of backtracking: maze array progressively showing '*' marks at (0,2), then (0,1), then (0,0) as the predecessor chain is followed from F back to S. Final maze shows the complete path marked.

title: Implementation - Dynamic 2D Array Allocation
summary: Explains how to allocate a 2D array dynamically in C/C++ using an array of pointers, since variable-size 2D arrays are not directly supported.
main_text: We clearly need a 2D structure for the maze. In C/C++ you cannot allocate a 2D array with variable size dimensions. The syntax 'new char[numrows][numcols]' is BAD and will not compile. The solution is a two-step allocation: first allocate 1 array of NUMROWS pointers, then loop through that array and allocate an array of NUMCOLS items for each row, putting its start address into the i-th pointer. For example, a char** m points to an array of 4 pointers (at addresses 1a0, 2c0, 1b4, 3e0), and each pointer points to a separately allocated row of 4 characters. This gives m the type char**, and access is via m[row][col]. The same approach is needed for the Visited array (int**) and Predecessor array (Location**).
notes_text: This is a critical implementation detail. The array of pointers pattern is the standard way to create dynamically-sized 2D arrays in C/C++. Each row is allocated separately on the heap, so the rows are not necessarily contiguous in memory, but indexing works the same as a static 2D array.

images.description: Diagram showing char** m pointing to an array of 4 pointers (rows), each pointing to a separately allocated array of 4 chars. Shows m[2] = 0x1b4 and m[2][1] = 0 access pattern. Adjacent diagrams show Visited and Predecessor arrays.

title: Implementation - Single 2D Array with Struct
summary: Shows alternative to multiple arrays: package maze char, visited flag, and predecessor into a single struct and use one 2D array of structs.
main_text: Instead of maintaining multiple separate 2D arrays (maze, visited, predecessor), we could package all the necessary data in a new struct/object and make a single 2D array of that type. The left side shows the multiple arrays approach: separate Maze array (char), Visited array (int), and Predecessor array (Location). The right side shows the single array approach: each cell contains all three pieces of data (the maze character, visited flag, and predecessor coordinates) in one struct. For example, cell (0,0) would contain: char '.', visited=1, predecessor=(1,0). Cell (1,0) would contain: char 'S', visited=1, predecessor=(-1,-1). This approach keeps related data together and simplifies passing data between functions.
notes_text: The single-struct approach is cleaner from an object-oriented perspective and reduces the number of arrays to manage. However, both approaches work correctly. The choice depends on personal preference and project requirements.

images.description: Comparison: left shows three separate 2D arrays (Maze, Visited, Predecessor). Right shows a single 2D array where each cell contains all three data fields (char, visited int, predecessor Location).
labels: A Single 2D Array With All Necessary Data

title: Queue Class Interface
summary: Defines the Queue class API with add_to_back, remove_from_front, and is_empty methods, using a linked list of Location items.
main_text: The Queue class uses a linked list of LocItem nodes to store Location structs. The public API includes: Queue() constructor, ~Queue() destructor to release resources, void add_to_back(Location loc) to insert a new Location at the end/back of the list, Location remove_from_front() to return and remove the oldest Location not already extracted (returns a Location with row and col both set to -1 if the queue is empty), and bool is_empty() to check if the queue has been fully drained. The private data includes a LocItem* head_ pointer. Students may add other data members and private functions to improve runtime as needed. None of the public method signatures may be changed.
notes_text: The Queue class is a custom linked list implementation, not using the STL deque. Students implement the linked list operations themselves. Adding a tail pointer would make add_to_back O(1) instead of O(n).

title: Maze Class Interface
summary: Defines the Maze class with read_maze and print_maze methods, emphasizing OO principles like encapsulation and keeping data private.
main_text: The Maze class stores the maze and performs operations on the maze. The public interface includes: Maze() constructor, ~Maze() destructor, bool read_maze(char* filename) to initialize the maze from a given file (returns true if there was an error), and void print_maze() const to print the maze to cout. Students may add any other desired functions and must add private data members and functions. The design principles emphasize: add other data members and member functions as needed, apply good OO principles by storing as data members any information needed across multiple calls, keep data private, and create member functions to operate on the data rather than letting outside code operate on them.
notes_text: The Maze class encapsulates all maze-related functionality. The BFS solver should be a member function of the Maze class (or called by one), keeping the algorithm close to the data it operates on.

title: Good Design Principle 1 - Place Computation Where Data Is
summary: Teaches that computation (code operating on data) should be in the same object where the data resides, using member functions instead of getters.
main_text: Good Design Principle 1: Place the computation (code that operates on data) where the data is (i.e. in the object where the code resides). Use a member function to process the data versus returning the data OUTSIDE for a third party to process. This means if you have a class with private data, operations on that data should be methods of the class, not external functions that receive the data through getters.
notes_text: This is a fundamental OO design principle also known as 'Tell, Don't Ask'. Instead of asking an object for its data and operating on it externally, tell the object to perform the operation itself. This leads to better encapsulation and more maintainable code.

title: Place Data and Code Together - Example
summary: Contrasts bad design (returning internal data via getters) with good design (providing member functions that operate on the data internally).
main_text: The slide contrasts two GradeBook class designs. Bad design (marked with prohibition sign): the class exposes internal data through int* getScores() which returns a pointer to the private scores array. External code in main() uses this pointer to compute the average, accessing and iterating over internal data directly. Good design (marked with a star): the class provides a double computeAverage() member function. Internally, computeAverage() accesses the private scores array and _size member to compute and return the average. External code simply calls gb.computeAverage(). The good design keeps scores private and moves the computation inside the class where the data lives.
notes_text: Returning raw pointers to internal data breaks encapsulation and creates tight coupling. If the internal representation changes (e.g., from array to vector), all external code breaks. With the member function approach, only the class implementation needs to change.

images.description: Two code blocks side by side. Left (bad, with X): GradeBook with getScores() returning int*, and main() computing average externally. Right (good, with star): GradeBook with computeAverage() method, and main() simply calling gb.computeAverage().

title: Maze Class - Operations Should Be Member Functions
summary: Reinforces that all maze operations (BFS solver, etc.) should be member functions of the Maze class, following the principle of placing code with data.
main_text: So whatever operations you need to do on the maze should probably be part of the Maze class. This applies the design principle from the previous slide directly to the maze project. The BFS search, path reconstruction, and any other maze manipulation should be implemented as member functions of the Maze class, not as external functions that receive maze data through parameters. The Maze class declaration is shown again with its public interface (Maze(), ~Maze(), read_maze, print_maze) and private section where students should add data members and functions.
notes_text: This is a direct application of the 'place computation where data is' principle. The Maze class should contain the 2D maze array, visited array, predecessor array, and all BFS logic as private members and methods.

title: Read Maze and Error Checking [1] - The Problem
summary: Identifies the error checking challenge: read_maze returns bool but multiple error types exist, and a single bool cannot distinguish between them.
main_text: A common issue with the read_maze() function: it returns a bool, but there may be multiple errors you want to check for (file not found, invalid characters, missing start/finish, etc.). The problem is a bool does NOT let you distinguish which error occurred. The question is: what options do we have to report specific error types? This leads to exploring different approaches for richer error reporting while maintaining or working within the existing API constraints.
notes_text: Error handling design is an important software engineering consideration. The limitations of a bool return type for error reporting motivate more sophisticated approaches like error codes, enums, or separate error-checking methods.

title: Read Maze and Error Checking [2] - Integer/Enum Approach
summary: If allowed to change the return type, use an integer error code or an enum like MazeErrors with values BAD_FILE, INVALID_CHAR to distinguish error types.
main_text: If you ARE allowed to change the return type (check the writeup or ask the professor), there are better options. Return an integer code where different values represent different errors, or better yet, define an enum in the class for the different error cases and return one of those values. For example: enum MazeErrors {BAD_FILE, INVALID_CHAR, ...}; This approach provides named, self-documenting error codes that callers can switch on to handle different error types differently.
notes_text: Enums are preferred over raw integers because they provide meaningful names and type safety. The caller can use a switch statement on the returned enum value to handle each error case appropriately.

title: Read Maze and Error Checking [3] - Separate Check Function
summary: If not allowed to change read_maze's return type, add a separate check_errors() method that returns an enum, keeping the bool API intact.
main_text: If you are NOT allowed to change the return type (check the writeup or ask the professor), the preferred approach is to create another member function to check for the various error conditions and let it return an integer code or enum. For example, add: enum MazeErrors check_errors() const; to the Maze class. This function examines the maze data after read_maze() completes and returns an enum indicating which (if any) error was found. This keeps the read_maze() bool API intact while providing richer error information through a separate method.
notes_text: This pattern of separating error detection from error reporting is common in software design. It allows the original API to remain unchanged while adding new capabilities.

title: Read Maze and Error Checking [4] - Getter Approach
summary: Alternative error checking approach using data members set by read_maze and getter functions to retrieve specific error statuses.
main_text: An alternate approach uses other data members and getter functions. Remember that data members can be set by one function and read/used by another. The read_maze() function can set one or more private data members with appropriate status during execution. Then getter functions can be called after read_maze() is finished to get the error status. For example, add to the Maze class: bool get_invalid_char_error() const and bool get_bad_start_finish() const as public getters, with corresponding private members bool invalidCharError_ and bool badStartFinish_. The read_maze() function sets these flags when it encounters errors, and the caller queries them after read_maze() returns.
notes_text: This getter approach is more granular than the enum approach, allowing multiple error conditions to be reported simultaneously. Each error type gets its own boolean flag and getter function.

title: Other Classes - File Organization
summary: Notes that additional classes may be introduced but all classes must be placed in maze.h and maze.cpp for compilation compatibility.
main_text: You may introduce other classes (such as the Queue class, Location struct, etc.) but must put all the classes in maze.h and maze.cpp so that the grading scripts will compile them all correctly. This file organization constraint ensures that the automated testing infrastructure can find and compile all necessary code.
notes_text: Keeping all classes in two files (header and implementation) simplifies the build process for the grading system, though in a real project you might separate each class into its own .h/.cpp pair.

title: Implementation Notes Section Divider
summary: Section divider transitioning to implementation notes for the maze project.
main_text: This is a section divider slide marking the transition to Implementation Notes. The following slides cover practical implementation details for the maze project including queue implementation, 2D array allocation, and code organization.
notes_text: The implementation notes provide practical guidance for completing the maze project assignment.

title: Code and Data Together
summary: Reinforces the principle that code and data should be kept together in the same class for good object-oriented design.
main_text: This slide reinforces the principle of keeping code and data together in the maze project implementation. All data related to the maze (the character array, visited array, predecessor array, dimensions) and all operations on the maze (reading, solving, printing, backtracking) should be encapsulated within the Maze class.
notes_text: This principle applies throughout the project: the Queue class encapsulates its linked list data and operations, and the Maze class encapsulates its grid data and algorithms.

title: Queue Implementation - Array-Based Alternative
summary: Describes an array-based queue alternative using front and back index pointers to track the active portion of a fixed-size array.
main_text: For the Queue class implementation, an alternative to a linked list is to make the internal array of size equal to the max number of squares (rows * cols). The question of whether it should be dynamic depends on whether the size is known at compile time (it is not, since the maze dimensions come from the file). We need to keep track of the front and back of the active portion of the array, since only part of the array is in use at any time. Just use integer indexes to record where the front and back are. The diagram shows the queue array with elements [1,0], [0,0], [2,0], [0,1], [3,0] with front=3 and back=5, indicating that elements at indices 0-2 have already been dequeued.
notes_text: The array-based queue is simpler to implement than a linked list but wastes memory since dequeued elements leave unused space at the front. For the maze project, the maximum queue size is bounded by the total number of cells, so the array can be pre-allocated.

images.description: Queue shown as an array with front=3 and back=5 index pointers. Elements at indices 0-2 are grayed out (dequeued), elements at 3-4 are active. Accompanied by maze state, visited array, and predecessor array.

title: 2D Array Allocation for Maze Implementation
summary: Reiterates the two-step dynamic 2D array allocation needed for maze, visited, and predecessor arrays with variable dimensions.
main_text: To allocate 2D arrays for maze, visited, and predecessor data structures: Note that in C/C++ you cannot allocate a 2D array with variable size dimensions (new char[numrows][numcols] is BAD). The solution is to allocate 1 array of NUMROWS pointers, then loop through that array and allocate an array of NUMCOLS items, placing each start address in the corresponding pointer. The diagram shows char** m pointing to an array of 4 row pointers (at addresses 1a0, 2c0, 1b4, 3e0), each pointing to a separately allocated row of 4 elements. Access is via m[row][col], for example m[2] = 0x1b4 and m[2][1] = 0.
notes_text: This allocation pattern must be applied three times in the project: once for the maze char array, once for the visited int array, and once for the predecessor array (or just once if using the single-struct approach).

images.description: Diagram showing two-step 2D array allocation: m (char**) points to array of 4 pointers, each pointing to a row of 4 chars. Shows the maze grid populated with S, #, F, ., etc.
labels: Each allocated on a separate iteration

title: Code Organization - read_maze Function
summary: Illustrates how read_maze should work: read maze file dimensions and contents, dynamically allocate 2D array, and return populated data to caller.
main_text: The code organization slide illustrates how read_maze() should work in a procedural (non-OO) version. Before calling read_maze(), main() has variables: filename='maze1.txt', numrows=???, numcols=???, maze=???. The read_maze function signature is: char** read_maze(char* filename, int* rows, int* cols). It opens the file with ifstream, reads the dimensions (3 rows, 5 cols), allocates the 2D char array dynamically, reads the maze characters into the array, and returns the char** pointer. After read_maze() returns, main() has: numrows=3, numcols=5, maze=300 (pointer to the allocated array). The 2D array at address 300 contains the maze data. A print_maze function takes char** maze, int rows, int cols to display the maze.
notes_text: In the OO version (Maze class), read_maze is a member function and the maze array, numrows, numcols are private data members, eliminating the need for pointer parameters. The procedural version shown here illustrates the underlying mechanics.

images.description: Complete diagram showing: main() stack frame before and after read_maze(), the file maze1.txt content, ifstream reading data, and the resulting 2D array at address 300 with row pointers and maze data.

title: Connected Components Project - BFS for Image Labeling
summary: Shows another BFS application: connected components labeling in images, using BFS to identify and label connected groups of foreground pixels.
main_text: The Connected Components Project applies BFS to image processing. As we find a foreground pixel, we start a BFS from it. We must visit the 8-connected neighbors (N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W, NW) unlike the maze which uses only 4-connected neighbors. We use a label array to track pixels we have already visited and labeled. The input is a 3D image array (rows x cols x color channels) and the output is a 2D label array where each connected component gets a unique integer label. The process: scan the image left-to-right, top-to-bottom. When an unlabeled foreground pixel is found, start a BFS that labels all connected foreground pixels with the same component number. The diagrams show: an input image with colored regions, the corresponding label array with -1 for background and component numbers (0, 1, 2) for foreground groups, and the progressive BFS labeling process.
notes_text: Connected components labeling is a fundamental computer vision algorithm. It demonstrates that BFS is not limited to pathfinding but applies to any problem where we need to explore connected regions of a graph or grid.

images.description: Four panels showing: input image grid with colored pixel groups, label array with component numbers, BFS exploration arrow pattern, and progressive labeling state with -1 for background and 0/1/2 for components.
